resources.string: How bone marrow makes blood cells
Blood cell formation in bone marrow

A qualitative view of normal adult human blood cell formation in red marrow. The illustrated branches show selected outcomes, not a fixed hierarchy or every lineage. Sizes and timing are not to scale.
In red marrow between bony trabeculae, nearby stromal cells and blood vessels help maintain blood-forming stem cells. These surroundings are part of the stem cell niche.
When a blood-forming stem cell divides, a daughter cell can retain stem cell identity. The division shown adds to the stem cell pool; not every division has this outcome.

As cells commit to a lineage, the kinds of blood cells they can produce become more limited. Two examples are the red cell lineage and the megakaryocyte lineage, which produces platelets. The cells at the ends of the branches are not immediate daughters of the stem cell.
A red cell precursor loses its nucleus
Along the red cell lineage, erythroblasts become smaller and their nuclei condense. A late erythroblast expels its nucleus, leaving a young red cell called a reticulocyte.
Young red cells enter the bloodstream
Reticulocytes cross the lining of a marrow sinusoid and are carried away by the flowing blood. They continue maturing in circulation.
